prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, There, Once

outputs.L1:
I passed through when I should have paused—there were a hundred doors, and one opened. Within, someone whose name I do not yet know was living out his middle years in modest terms: two chairs, one place set for an early breakfast, one plate bearing dry toast and softening butter. There his mind raced through writings memorized long ago, as he struggled to collect himself.

In his youth, he had studied with devotion the corners of old paintings—the intricate matrices of fields and towns, passages both elaborate and precise: wheat, columns, figures against ground, all classically proportioned along lines meant, eventually, to converge at a vanishing point. Yet they continued on regardless; they troubled the eye.

He had amassed sets of books printed in the nineteenth century, their pages stiff and unyielding—memoirs of poets, engravings of rustic private subjects set against times of public unrest, frescoes of human strangeness rendered in gatefold prints.

"Why does this go on chastening me?" he asks, to no one in particular. And yet it does. There is a painful error in this act of setting something down, of saying aloud, "it is nothing yet," when he had meant to say *nothing at all*—but then nothing peered through the keyhole, and nothing took possession.

Snow lay upon the roofs, snow lingered in traces on the ground. Passersby, their trouser-cuffs damp, kept their eyes upon the pavement as the hill climbed before them, while light gathered in the river and slowly, steadily, spread.
outputs.L2:
I walked by without stopping, though I shouldn't have—countless doors lined the way. One swung open. Behind it, a man whose identity remains unknown to me was living out his later years modestly: a pair of chairs, a single breakfast setting, one plate holding stale toast and melting butter. His thoughts spun through texts committed to memory years before, as he struggled to compose himself. In his younger days, he had lovingly studied the margins of antique paintings—the intricate grids of countryside and settlements, detailed and specific scenes of grain fields, columns, human figures against their backdrops, all rendered in classical proportion, lines destined to converge somewhere at their vanishing point. Yet they kept going regardless, unsettling to behold. He amassed volumes printed in the eighteen-hundreds, their pages stiff with age, poets' memoirs, illustrations of quiet country scenes from eras of widespread civic distress, depictions of human peculiarity spread across fold-out prints.

"Why does this keep humbling me?" he asks, though no one listens. Yet it does. There's an anguish in this act of recording, of speaking the words "it is nothing yet" when he had intended something else entirely—only for nothing to appear, glimpsed through the keyhole, nothing claiming its territory. Snow covered the rooftops, faint traces of it lingered on the earth below, while people walked past with damp cuffs, eyes fixed on the pavement as it climbed the slope, and light collected in the river before slowly spreading outward.
outputs.L3:
I moved through door after door of possibility, each one yielding to my touch and then closing again, revealing nothing, until at last a single door opened and stayed open. Behind it was a man—unnamed, unremarkable in the way that middle age can render a person unremarkable, his life organized around small and unspectacular rituals. A single place was set at his breakfast table each morning, the same cup, the same worn spot on the table where his elbow had rested for years. There was nothing in this arrangement that spoke of drama; it was simply the architecture of a life lived alone, sustained by habit rather than by any particular hope.

As he sat, his mind would not be still. Fragments of memorized writings surfaced unbidden—lines of poetry half-recalled, phrases from books read decades ago, the residue of an education that had never quite left him. He struggled against this static, trying to gather himself, to press these fragments into some kind of order, but they resisted him, circling and receding like objects glimpsed underwater. He would sit for long minutes simply attempting to compose his thoughts into something resembling clarity, and often failing.

In this effort, his mind would inevitably drift backward, to his youth, when he had given himself over entirely to the study of old paintings. He had pored over their surfaces with an intensity that bordered on devotion, tracing the perspective lines that the old masters had drawn with such care, all of them reaching toward that single point where sight itself seemed to vanish. He had understood the mathematics of it, the logic that made a flat surface suggest depth, distance, the illusion of a world receding infinitely inward. And yet something in this had always troubled him—some discrepancy between what the eye was told to see and what it actually saw, a faint dissonance he could never quite name, even after all these years of looking.

This same restlessness had led him, later in life, to collect books—specifically the memoirs of nineteenth-century poets, bound in leather that had softened and cracked with age, illustrated with engravings whose fine crosshatched lines seemed to hold light in a way that felt almost alive. He would take these volumes down from their shelves in the evenings, turning their brittle pages, and find himself chastened by them in some way he could never fully articulate. "Why does this trouble me so?" he would ask aloud, to no one, to the empty room, and the question would hang there, unanswered, dissolving into the silence of his apartment.

It was in these moments that a peculiar confusion would overtake him—the strange and painful sensation that arose when he meant only to say "nothing," to dismiss some thought or feeling as insignificant, and yet found that this nothing had begun to assume a shape, a presence, almost a weight in the room with him. It sat beside his unspoken words like an uninvited guest, refusing to be dismissed, refusing to remain merely an absence.

Outside, the snow continued to fall, softening the hard edges of the city, and the pavements below gleamed wetly under the streetlamps. Somewhere beyond the rooftops, dawn was beginning its slow arrival, spreading a pale and hesitant light across the surface of the river, illuminating nothing in particular, and yet changing, subtly, everything.
outputs.L4:
He had reached that particular latitude of life—not old, not young, but settled into the long plateau of the middle years—where afternoons seemed to arrive already carrying the weight of evening. He sat now in the chair by the window, the one with the worn left armrest, and allowed his mind to wander back through the rooms of his memory the way a man might walk through a house he no longer owned but still held the keys to.

There had been the years of looking at paintings. Not studying them, exactly—he had never been a scholar of art in any formal sense—but looking, the way one looks at weather, or at a face across a room one keeps returning to. He remembered a particular afternoon in a museum whose name he had since forgotten, standing before a canvas where a corridor of columns receded into a golden vanishing point, and feeling something in his chest tighten and release, as if the painting had located a doorway in him he hadn't known was there. He had been young then, still filling notebooks with sketches of converging lines, still convinced that if he practiced enough he could learn to make the world recede properly on paper—could learn the exact geometry by which nearness became distance, presence became suggestion.

He thought of the antique books too, the smell of them, that particular dust-and-leather perfume that seemed to carry the accumulated breath of everyone who had ever opened them before him. He had collected a modest shelf of these once, mostly volumes on optics and drawing, treatises with diagrams of eyes and light rays and the mathematics of illusion. He had loved them not for their content, which he only half understood, but for their patience—the sense that someone, long ago, had sat exactly as he now sat, trying to fix something fleeting into permanence, and had failed in some beautiful, forgivable way.

All of this rose in him now, not as narrative but as texture, as the general hum beneath a life. And beneath that hum, he became aware of something else—a thought that had not yet become a thought, a pressure at the base of his throat that wanted to resolve into words but would not. He tried, sitting there, to give it shape. He opened his mouth slightly, as if testing the air, as if the thought might complete itself the moment breath moved through it. But nothing came. Or rather: something did come, but it was the shape of nothing, an absence dressed up as an utterance, a silence that had the contours of speech without the substance.

He sat with this for a long moment. It was not quite frightening, but it was not quite comfortable either—this sensation of reaching for the innermost fact of his own existence and finding, instead of a fact, a kind of clearing. A vanishing point, he thought, with a small and private irony. All those years learning how lines converge into absence on the page, and now his own mind performed the same trick, unbidden, on him.

He almost laughed. He did not.

Instead he turned his attention, gently, to the window, where he found that it had begun to snow. The flakes came down without hurry, catching the pale afternoon light in a way that made them seem, for an instant each, individually lit—small suspended sparks before they settled onto the sill, the street, the shoulders of a woman walking briskly below with her collar turned up against the cold. A man passed her going the other way, his breath visible, his pace unbothered by whatever weight he carried or didn't carry within him. Somewhere out of sight, a child laughed at something, a short bright sound swallowed almost instantly by the muffling snow.

The man at the window watched all of this without trying to make it mean anything. The thought that had refused to complete itself did not return, or if it did, it no longer asked to be spoken. The snow continued to fall. The light held its pale, indifferent glow. The passersby went on toward wherever they were going, unaware of the man in the window, unaware of his years of paintings and books and careful studies of how things recede, unaware that for a moment he had touched the edge of something and found only stillness there—

and that the stillness, it turned out, was enough. The world outside kept moving, kept snowing, kept indifferent to whether he had found his words or not, and in this indifference there was, unexpectedly, something like peace.
outputs.L5:
# On Beginnings

Once, there was a moment—just one—when everything could have gone differently. We rarely notice these moments as they happen; they slip past disguised as ordinary Tuesdays or unremarkable conversations. Only later, looking back, do we recognize them for what they were: hinges upon which entire lives turned.

There is something profound in the smallness of beginnings. One decision, one word spoken or withheld, one chance encounter—these are the seeds from which vast forests eventually grow. We tend to imagine that significant changes require significant causes, but history and memory both suggest otherwise. Empires have fallen because of one miscalculation. Friendships have formed because of one chance meeting on a rainy street corner.

Once we accept this truth, we start to see our own lives differently. There, in that conversation you almost didn't have. There, in that book you almost didn't pick up. One choice, seemingly insignificant, sets into motion a chain of consequences that ripples outward, touching lives you may never even know about.

Perhaps this is why storytellers so often begin with "once"—once upon a time, once there was a person who dared to dream. The word carries within it both distance and intimacy, gesturing toward something that happened and yet remains alive in the telling. It suggests that the past is not truly past, that there is always a thread connecting then to now, one continuous story rather than a series of disconnected events.

In the end, we are all just chapters in longer books, each of us representing one small but essential moment in vast, unfolding narratives—stories that began once, long before we arrived, and will continue on, there, long after we're gone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary piece in the style of a modernist writer, exploring themes of missed opportunities and quiet domestic solitude, with imagery of doors, breakfast, and old paintings.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Room Where the Light Comes Late**

The door did not close so much as settle, the way old doors do, sighing into their frames as though tired of the argument between open and shut. She had painted it green once—a green like the underside of a leaf—and now, in the gray hour before the toast burned, it had faded to the color of something remembered rather than seen.

Breakfast was two eggs, always two, though there had been years when it might have been more: a child's spoon, a second cup, someone else's hand reaching for the marmalade before she could offer it. The eggs sat white and blind in their saucers. Outside, the milkman's cart made its small thunder and was gone, and she thought, not for the first time, how the whole of a life could be measured in the space between one sound and its absence.

Above the sideboard hung the painting—her mother's, or her mother's mother's, no one now living could say which. A woman in a doorway, half-turned, her hand upon the frame as if she meant to leave the canvas altogether, as if three hundred years of paint might finally give way to something like motion. The light in the painting fell the way light falls in November, apologetic, unwilling to commit itself to either warmth or shadow. She had looked at that painting every morning for eleven years and had never once decided whether the woman was arriving or departing.

There had been a man once—there is always a man once, in stories like this, though he does not deserve so grand a pronoun. He had stood in this very doorway (not the painted one, the real one, though by now the two had begun to blur, the way two rooms will blur when you have stared too long at both) and he had said something about trains, about the hour, about how he really ought to be going. And she had let him go. That was the whole of it. She had let him go the way one lets go of a held breath, without ceremony, without knowing until afterward that something had been required of her and she had not given it.

The toast burned. It always burned a little; she had come to prefer it that way, the bitterness a kind of company.

She ate at the small table by the window, where the door was visible in her periphery—always visible, always slightly ajar, as though the house itself could not decide whether to invite the day in or keep it out on the step, shivering, uninvited. Somewhere beyond the glass the year was turning, indifferent, the sycamore letting go of its leaves one at a time as though counting something down.

The woman in the painting continued her turning, her eternal half-completed gesture. Sometimes, in the particular slant of afternoon light, it seemed she might finish it—might step from the frame entirely and cross the room and say the thing that wanted saying. But the light shifted, as light does, and the woman remained where she had always been, one hand on the frame, forever on the threshold of a decision already made and unmade a thousand times.

The clock in the hall gave its small apologetic chime. Another hour arriving to replace the one just spent.

She rose, eventually, and washed the two plates, the two cups, and dried them with the same cloth she had used for years, its pattern worn to a memory of flowers. The door stayed as it was—not quite open, not quite closed—admitting a thin blade of morning that fell across the floor and touched, briefly, the hem of the painted woman's gown, before the sun moved on, indifferent, to other rooms, other doorways, other unfinished departures.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental narrative fragment that blends the perspective of an unnamed man with meditations on art, memory, and the passage of time, ending with a snowy urban scene.
counterfactuals.output:
He had been standing before the painting for eleven minutes—he knew this because he had checked his watch upon entering, a habit inherited from his father, who believed that time spent looking was time that should be accounted for, measured, justified. The painting was small, unremarkable to most who passed through the gallery that afternoon: a woman at a window, her back to the viewer, light falling across floorboards in a manner that suggested late morning, or perhaps the specific gold of October.

He thought: *this is what happens to time when someone decides to keep it.*

The artist had been dead for three centuries. This fact did nothing to diminish the woman's posture, the particular slope of her shoulders that suggested she was waiting for something, or had just finished waiting, the distinction between these two states being, he realized, the entire problem of memory itself. Was she anticipating a letter, a lover, the simple return of afternoon light through different weather? Or was she already remembering—already turning the moment into something smaller, portable, capable of being carried into whatever came next?

He did not know why he had come to this city, why his feet had carried him into this particular building on this particular gray Tuesday. There had been a woman once, in his own life, who stood at windows this way, and he had thought, at the time, that he understood her stillness. He had been wrong. He understood now that he had only been looking at his own reflection in the glass, mistaking it for hers.

Memory, he thought, is a kind of forgery. We paint over the original so many times that eventually we cannot say which layer was true, or if truth was ever the point. The restorers who worked on paintings like this one—stripping away centuries of yellowed varnish, careful as surgeons—often found that what lay beneath was not more vivid but more strange: colors the original audience never saw, gestures that had been softened by time's accumulating haze. Perhaps this was mercy. Perhaps the varnish was its own kind of love.

He left the gallery without buying a postcard, without recording the artist's name in the small notebook he carried for such purposes. Some things, he had decided, should remain unfixed, floating free of documentation, available only to memory's imperfect custody.

Outside, snow had begun to fall—not the announced snow of forecasts and warnings, but the quiet, almost apologetic kind that arrives without ceremony, settling on shoulders and awnings and the black iron rails of the museum steps. The city had gone soft at its edges. Streetlamps wore haloes. A bus idled at the corner, its windows fogged with the breath of unseen passengers, becoming for a moment something like the woman in the painting: present, contained, facing away from him toward whatever waited on the other side of the glass.

He stood there a long moment, watching his own breath disappear into the whitening air, and thought that this too was a kind of painting—one that would not survive the hour, that no restorer would ever try to save. And yet here it was: the snow falling on the black branches of the trees lining the avenue, the yellow windows of apartments blinking on one by one like slow returning memories, the whole city arranging itself into something that might, if he did not look too closely, resemble stillness.

He did not check his watch this time. Some moments, he understood, were meant to pass unaccounted for—already becoming, even as he stood within them, the thing he would later try, and fail, to remember exactly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, imagistic prose poem exploring regret and creative frustration, incorporating references to nineteenth-century books, engravings, and vanishing points in classical painting.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Vanishing Point

I keep the nineteenth century in a drawer that won't quite close—foxed pages, the smell of someone else's basement, engravings where every line was cut by a hand now dust. Look how the burin trembled once, then didn't. Look how the cross-hatching builds a shadow out of nothing but refusal, thousands of tiny abstentions making a darkness deep enough to drown in.

This is what regret is: a technique for accumulating absence until it resembles form.

I wanted to write the book that unfolds like Piranesi's prisons, each room a lie about scale, staircases that go nowhere on purpose. Instead I have this—a paragraph that keeps circling back to apologize for itself, ink pooling at the nib like blood that won't clot into sentence. The engraver's error is invisible until you know where to look: a wrong perspective line, someone's assistant miscalculating the point where all parallels agree to die.

In classical composition the eye is dragged, gently, toward a single throat of vanishing—every road, every colonnade, every mourner's downturned face aimed like an arrow at the place where the world admits it cannot be depicted anymore. That's where I keep finding myself. Not at the horizon. Behind it, in the fold where the canvas becomes only canvas, gesso and rabbit-skin glue, no more sky to promise.

I think of Hardy's endings, how he'd let the machinery of plot grind a woman down slow, the prose almost tender about it, a scalpel dressed in Sunday clothes. I think of how many times I have been both the hand that holds the knife and the paper that receives the cut, unable to tell anymore which one made the choice.

The frustration is not that the work resists me. It's that it doesn't—that it lies down instantly, offers its throat, and still I fumble the incision, still I engrave the wrong shadow into the plate, still I set the vanishing point too close, so everything rushes toward a center that was never earned, a false intimacy, a horizon collapsed into the width of my own doubt.

Somewhere Doré is still burning the underworld into boxwood, each flame a controlled disaster, a wound made permanent by acid and pressure. I want that permanence. I want the mistake to become a style, the way certain broken bindings now look intentional, an aesthetic of endurance rather than neglect. But I know the difference between a scar earned by time and a wound I keep reopening because I mistake the pain for progress.

Regret has its own vanishing point too—a place behind the years where all my unwritten drafts converge, agree to become one silence, one page that was always blank, dressed up in the memory of ink. I go there some nights. I stand exactly where the lines would meet if I extended them far enough, and I watch the world I meant to make recede correctly, beautifully, according to all the old rules of perspective—every failure in flawless, aching proportion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal, introspective monologue about a man haunted by his own artistic ambitions, weaving together sensory details of a modest home and a wintry cityscape outside.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Unfinished Things

The radiator ticks like a metronome for a symphony no one will ever compose. I sit here in this room—my room, though tonight it feels borrowed, feels like a coat someone else left behind—and I listen to the building breathe. Somewhere below me, water moves through pipes older than my grandfather's grief. Somewhere above, a woman drops something heavy and I flinch as if it were my own heart hitting the floor.

The window is a mouth of frost, and beyond it the city has turned the color of old bone. Snow doesn't fall so much as *arrive*, already exhausted, settling on the fire escapes like ash from a fire I keep meaning to light. I press my palm to the glass and the cold answers back, patient, the way failure always is—never urgent, never cruel, just *waiting*, the way a canvas waits, blank and insufferably polite.

I was going to be someone. Wasn't I? There's a version of me still out there in the snow, walking through it in a coat I never bought, carrying a portfolio full of paintings I never made. I see him sometimes, crossing under the streetlamp, and he doesn't look back because he doesn't know I exist. He's the one who finished things. He's the one whose hands don't shake.

The kettle on the stove is beginning its low complaint. Steam will fog the window further, erase the city entirely, leave me with just this room—the peeling wallpaper with its faded roses, blooming and dying in the same breath; the lamp that flickers like it's trying to remember a word; the shelf of books I've read halfway, their spines cracked at the exact point where I lost my nerve.

I could have been a sculptor. I could have carved my ambition out of marble instead of letting it curdle into this—this sitting, this waiting, this watching snow bury the city in soft, indifferent judgment. Somewhere in this apartment is a stack of pages, half-written, half-loved, and I can hear them from here, rustling like they're trying to whisper the ending I never gave them.

The clock says it's almost midnight, though time in this room moves like syrup, thick and slow and unwilling to commit. I could open the window. I could let the cold in, let it finish what I started—this slow erasure, this quiet failure to become. But instead I only watch. Only breathe. Only listen to the tick of the radiator, the drop of snow, the whisper of pages I'll never finish, in a city that has already forgotten to expect anything from me at all.

Outside, that other man—the one who finished things—turns the corner and is gone. And I remain, haunted by the ghost of what I might have made, in this small, modest room, where even the silence has begun to sound like art I failed to create.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
